last_attempts_log.asr_text: On my morning commute, I open a news app's For You page and find stories that fit what I follow. It uses my interests, followed sources, and past activity on Google services and YouTube. I don't have to search through everything before work. I can follow topics, ask for more or less of a subject, or hide a source. I cannot see every signal behind the order, but I can adjust the feed when I have time. Most days, I feel up to date.

On my phone, I keep seeing the same stories, arguments, and sources. I start to wonder if my world is getting smaller without my permission. I want to know why one item appears above another, but I cannot change the system's hidden settings. I worry the feed may be tuned for clicks and advertising, not only to help me understand the news. In an analysis of more than 10 million U.S. users, feed ranking reduced exposure to different political sides, though users' own clicks played an even larger role. During the election period studied, like-minded sources made up most of what active adults saw.
Each morning, a commuter opens a news feed between stops. Stories linked to recent interests appear first, while other news stays out of sight.
For one reader, this is a shortcut through an endless stream. For another, the same sorting raises a harder question: What might never reach the screen?

Both readers share one belief: what appears on screen shapes what they understand and how well news fits their daily life. But the stakes split. One needs relevant news within limited time. The other fears being closed inside a narrow view without noticing. One experiences ranking as partly her choice—follow this, hide that. The other faces rules she cannot see. In short experiments, some political attitudes did not measurably change, while effects building over years remained outside those tests. Their wishes do not make one simple answer.

The deeper issue is not simply whether personalized news is good or bad; it is who gets to define what counts as relevant and how visible that power is to the person reading. Convenience is not only about speed; it also arrives with a hidden shape, and that shape is part of the news experience itself.
